question: The circadian rhythm is best described as:

options.text: A rhythm with no fixed period, varying randomly from day to day
An internal biological clock, roughly 24 hours long, that governs the natural cycle of alertness, body temperature and sleepiness
A cycle that is entirely imposed by external light and has no internal biological basis
A pattern that only affects digestion, not alertness or sleep

explanation: The body runs an internal clock close to 24 hours, which drives predictable daily swings in alertness, core body temperature and the drive to sleep — normally kept in step with the day-night cycle by light exposure and routine, but capable of drifting out of sync when that routine is disrupted.

question: The period of lowest alertness and performance in most people's circadian cycle, often called the "window of circadian low", typically falls:

options.text: At a time that varies with no consistent pattern between individuals
Immediately after waking, at any time of day
In the middle of the afternoon, around 15:00
In the early hours of the morning, broadly between about 02:00 and 06:00

explanation: For most people, core body temperature and alertness both reach their daily low point in the early hours of the morning, which is why this window is specifically associated with reduced performance, more errors, and why its timing matters so much for scheduling long night duties.

question: Besides the early-morning circadian low, many people also experience a smaller dip in alertness known as the "post-lunch dip", occurring:

options.text: In the early-to-mid afternoon, independent of whether a large meal was actually eaten
Only immediately after waking in the morning
Exclusively in people who have eaten a heavy lunch
At exactly the same time as the early-morning circadian low

explanation: The early-afternoon dip in alertness is largely a circadian effect rather than purely a consequence of eating, since it occurs on a similar schedule even on days with little or no lunch — though a heavy meal can make the dip feel more pronounced.

question: A full night's sleep is normally made up of repeating cycles of different stages, broadly dividing into:

options.text: Stages that occur in a completely random order each night
Only REM sleep, with no other stage present
Non-REM sleep (including deep, slow-wave sleep) and REM sleep, alternating in cycles through the night
A single, unchanging stage lasting the whole night

explanation: Sleep progresses through repeating cycles of non-REM stages (including deep, slow-wave sleep) and REM sleep, each cycle lasting roughly ninety minutes, with the balance between stages shifting over the course of the night.

question: Deep, slow-wave sleep (the most physically restorative stage) is concentrated mainly:

options.text: In the earlier part of the night's sleep, with REM sleep becoming more prominent later
Only in the final hour before waking
Equally throughout the entire night, with no particular concentration
Exclusively during a short daytime nap, never at night

explanation: Deep sleep makes up a larger share of the earlier sleep cycles, while REM sleep's share grows through the night — which is one reason a sleep period cut short at the end still captures a reasonable amount of deep, restorative sleep, even though it loses the later REM-heavy stages.

question: A "microsleep" refers to:

options.text: A brief, involuntary episode of actual sleep lasting a few seconds, which can occur even while a person believes they are still awake
A condition that cannot occur in a trained, alert pilot
A type of dream that only occurs during REM sleep
A deliberate, planned short nap of around twenty minutes

explanation: A microsleep is involuntary and brief — a few seconds of genuine sleep that intrudes on wakefulness, often without the person even realising it happened — and is a particular hazard when it occurs during a task requiring continuous attention, such as monitoring instruments or a long drive.

question: A short, deliberately timed nap (sometimes called a "power nap") is generally recommended to be kept brief, typically under about 20-30 minutes, mainly to:

options.text: Make the nap last exactly as long as a full sleep cycle
Prevent any sleep from occurring at all during the nap
Avoid waking from deep, slow-wave sleep, which tends to leave a person groggy and impaired for some time afterward (sleep inertia)
Guarantee that no sleep inertia can ever occur regardless of nap length

explanation: If a nap runs long enough to reach deep, slow-wave sleep, waking up from that stage tends to produce sleep inertia — a period of grogginess and impaired performance — which is why naps intended to restore alertness quickly are usually kept short enough to stay out of deep sleep.

question: Jet lag following a long flight across several time zones occurs because:

options.text: The body's circadian clock adjusts to a new time zone within a few minutes of landing
The circadian clock has no role in jet lag at all
The internal circadian clock cannot instantly re-synchronise to the new local time, leaving it temporarily out of step with the destination's day-night cycle
Jet lag is caused purely by cabin pressurization, unrelated to time zones

explanation: The internal clock re-adjusts to a new time zone only gradually, typically needing roughly a day for each time zone crossed, so for several days after a long crossing it keeps signalling alertness and sleepiness on something closer to the old schedule than the new one.

question: Most people find it easier to adjust to flying westward (effectively lengthening their day) than to flying eastward (effectively shortening it) across the same number of time zones, mainly because:

options.text: The body's clock adjusts identically regardless of direction
The internal circadian clock naturally runs slightly longer than 24 hours, making it easier to delay (push later) than to advance (pull earlier)
Eastward flights are always physically longer in flight time than westward flights
Westward flights involve crossing more time zones on average

explanation: Because the free-running circadian cycle tends to be a little longer than 24 hours, staying up later (delaying the clock, as westward travel requires) tends to come more naturally than going to bed and waking earlier (advancing the clock, as eastward travel requires) — a well-established asymmetry in how people adapt to time zone changes.

question: Rotating shift patterns (where duty times change frequently, such as alternating between day and night duties) are generally considered more fatiguing than a fixed schedule mainly because they:

options.text: Repeatedly disrupt the circadian clock's ability to settle into a stable rhythm before it has to shift again
Have no effect on the circadian clock whatsoever
Are equally well tolerated by every individual with no variation
Always provide more total sleep opportunity than a fixed schedule

explanation: Just as crossing time zones takes time to adjust to, each change of shift pattern asks the circadian clock to re-settle, and a rotating schedule keeps asking for that adjustment before it has properly completed — a cumulative strain a stable schedule does not impose.

question: Good "sleep hygiene" practices, recommended to support reliable sleep, typically include:

options.text: Keeping a consistent sleep schedule where possible, and sleeping in a dark, cool, quiet environment
Varying bedtime by several hours every night to "keep the body guessing"
Consuming caffeine shortly before going to bed
Using a brightly lit, noisy room to fall asleep faster

explanation: Consistency and a sleep-friendly environment both support the circadian system and ease the process of falling and staying asleep; irregular timing, light, noise and stimulants close to bedtime all work against it.

question: Although alcohol can make a person fall asleep more quickly, its overall effect on sleep quality later in the night is to:

options.text: Uniformly improve sleep quality throughout the entire night
Disrupt normal sleep architecture, often leading to more fragmented, lighter sleep and reduced REM sleep in the second half of the night
Have no effect on sleep once the person has fallen asleep
Only affect sleep quality in people who rarely drink

explanation: Alcohol's sedative effect can shorten the time it takes to fall asleep, but as it is metabolised over the night it tends to fragment sleep and suppress REM sleep, leaving overall sleep quality worse than it would have been without it — which is why alcohol is not a reliable aid for genuinely restorative sleep before duty.

question: Obstructive sleep apnoea is a sleep disorder in which:

options.text: It has no link to daytime sleepiness or alertness
The upper airway repeatedly narrows or collapses during sleep, causing brief breathing interruptions and fragmented, poor-quality sleep despite adequate time in bed
Breathing becomes faster and deeper throughout the entire night with no interruption
A person is simply unable to fall asleep at all

explanation: Repeated airway narrowing or collapse during sleep causes brief arousals, often many times a night, that the person may not remember — the result is sleep that feels unrefreshing despite apparently normal time in bed, producing significant daytime sleepiness and reduced alertness.

question: Obstructive sleep apnoea is particularly relevant to aircrew medical fitness because it is strongly associated with:

options.text: Excessive daytime sleepiness, which directly raises the risk of microsleeps and impaired performance on duty
No measurable effect on daytime functioning whatsoever
A condition limited exclusively to children
Improved alertness during the day due to compensatory daytime sleep

explanation: The fragmented sleep that sleep apnoea causes translates directly into significant daytime sleepiness, which is exactly the kind of fatigue risk that makes the condition relevant to assessing fitness for safety-critical duties.

question: Acute fatigue, as distinct from chronic (cumulative) fatigue, is best described as:

options.text: Fatigue that only affects physical, never mental, performance
A condition with no relationship to sleep at all
Fatigue that builds up over weeks and cannot be relieved by a single night's sleep
Tiredness following a single period of exertion or sleep loss, which is normally resolved by one adequate period of rest or sleep

explanation: Acute fatigue is the ordinary, short-term tiredness that follows a long day or a poor night's sleep, and generally clears up with one good recovery sleep — in contrast to chronic fatigue, which accumulates over successive days of insufficient recovery.

question: Chronic (cumulative) fatigue builds up when:

options.text: It can always be fully resolved by one night of good sleep, regardless of how long it has built up
A single poor night's sleep is immediately followed by a full, adequate recovery sleep
A person repeatedly fails to get adequate recovery sleep over successive days, so a sleep debt accumulates faster than it is paid off
It only occurs after a single isolated night shift

explanation: Each night of insufficient sleep adds to a running deficit. If recovery sleep does not keep pace, the deficit accumulates over days or weeks into chronic fatigue, which — unlike acute fatigue — typically needs more than one good night to fully resolve.

question: Fatigue degrades vigilance (sustained attention to a monitoring task) mainly by:

options.text: Improving sustained attention the more tired a person becomes
Having no measurable effect on vigilance at any level of fatigue
Affecting only physical reaction time, never attention itself
Increasing the frequency and length of attention lapses and microsleeps the longer the monitoring task continues

explanation: As fatigue deepens, the brief lapses of attention and the risk of microsleeps both increase, particularly during long, low-stimulation monitoring tasks — exactly the combination (fatigue plus a quiet cruise phase) that makes fatigue management relevant to flight safety.

question: As people age, a commonly observed change in sleep pattern is:

options.text: Lighter, more fragmented sleep with a smaller proportion of deep, slow-wave sleep compared with younger adults
No change in sleep pattern at all across the lifespan
An increase in sleep need to well over ten hours a night for most older adults
A large increase in the total proportion of deep sleep compared with younger adults

explanation: Sleep tends to become lighter and more easily disrupted with age, with a reduced share of deep, slow-wave sleep, even though total nightly sleep need does not increase — a pattern worth recognising rather than assuming all ages experience sleep identically.

question: Before a known early-morning duty start, deliberately going to bed earlier than usual the night before is a useful sleep-planning strategy mainly because it:

options.text: Has no benefit, since total sleep time cannot be adjusted in advance
Guarantees falling asleep instantly regardless of the body's current circadian state
Builds in extra sleep opportunity ahead of a reduction expected from an early alarm, helping to limit the resulting sleep debt
Only works if the duty is a night shift rather than an early morning one

explanation: Anticipatory sleep — banking some extra rest ahead of a known period of reduced sleep opportunity — is a standard, practical fatigue-management technique, even though it does not fully substitute for sleep lost later and does not instantly override the circadian clock's own schedule.

question: Using a sedative or sleep aid to force sleep before a duty period carries a particular risk because:

options.text: Residual drowsiness (a "hangover" effect) from the medication can still be present and impair performance after waking, even once sleep itself has ended
Sedatives have no effect on sleep architecture or next-day alertness
All sleep aids clear from the body instantly upon waking
Sedatives are always preferable to natural sleep for aircrew

explanation: Many sleep medications remain active in the body well after waking, which can leave residual drowsiness or impaired reaction time that a person may not fully recognise in themselves — a reason such aids are approached cautiously, and only in line with the specific guidance that applies to flying duties.

question: Core body temperature and subjective alertness are closely linked across the day in that:

options.text: Body temperature and alertness have no relationship to each other
Body temperature stays perfectly constant throughout the day
Alertness is highest exactly when body temperature is at its daily minimum
Alertness tends to track body temperature's circadian rhythm closely, both reaching their lowest point at roughly the same time of the early morning

explanation: Both alertness and core body temperature follow a circadian pattern that peaks and troughs together, with the lowest body temperature of the day roughly coinciding with the window of lowest alertness in the early hours of the morning.

question: Fatigue affects decision making in a way that closely parallels the effects of stress described elsewhere in this subject, mainly by:

options.text: Only affecting mood, with no measurable effect on cognitive performance
Having a completely unrelated set of effects with no overlap with stress
Improving the speed of decision making while leaving accuracy unaffected
Narrowing attention, slowing information processing and reducing working memory capacity

explanation: Fatigue and stress both tend to degrade the same underlying resources — attention, working memory, flexible reasoning — which is why a fatigued crew member shows many of the same performance problems as a highly stressed one, even though the two causes are quite different.

question: A person's own subjective sense of how fatigued they are is known to be:

options.text: An imperfect guide — people can underestimate their own impairment, particularly as fatigue deepens
Unrelated to actual performance in any way
Always an overestimate of true impairment
A perfectly reliable and accurate measure of actual impairment at all times

explanation: Fatigue itself can blunt a person's ability to judge how impaired they actually are, which is part of why fatigue management relies on objective measures — rostering rules, duty time limits, planned rest — rather than solely on individuals reporting that they feel fine.

question: A controlled rest or "napping" policy, where one pilot takes a brief, planned rest in their seat during a long cruise while the other actively monitors, is intended to:

options.text: Have no connection to fatigue management at all
Address fatigue proactively by permitting a brief recovery sleep under controlled conditions, rather than risking an unplanned, unmonitored microsleep later
Replace the need for proper rest periods between duties entirely
Allow both pilots to sleep simultaneously with no one actively monitoring the aircraft

explanation: A controlled rest policy accepts that fatigue can develop even on a well-planned duty and manages it directly — a brief, structured, monitored rest for one pilot — rather than leaving fatigue to express itself later as an unplanned and unmonitored lapse.
